## TL;DR

This task adds accessible names to the Agents skills controls and records a keyboard and contrast QA pass for Work, Settings, Releases, and Agents. The earlier implementation and documentation are already committed on this task branch. The active handoff failure was administrative: the engineering report draft did not contain the required headings. This draft supplies those sections; no product code changed during this resumed turn.

## Work and rationale

The documented accessibility finding was in the Agents skills UI. The close control was rendered as an × glyph without a programmatic name, so a screen-reader user could not reliably identify its action. It now has the accessible name “Close dialog.” The skills-add control also previously relied on a `title`, which is not a dependable accessible name across assistive technology. It now exposes a role-specific name, “Add skills to <role>,” so repeated controls can be distinguished.

The regression coverage lives in `src/ui-app/tests/keyboard-a11y.test.ts`. It asserts both accessible names at the component-source level. The QA record at `docs/qa/2026-11-keyboard-a11y.md` describes a route-by-route keyboard pass and automated contrast results. The docs say that the first ten focus stops were traversed on Work, Settings, Releases, and Agents; on Agents, the Skills dialog retained focus during twelve Tab presses, closed with Escape, and restored focus to the invoking control. Releases Preview is an inline disclosure, so Escape did not close it. These details are retained as the evidence recorded by the earlier QA run, rather than being presented as observations newly made in this resumed session.

The QA note reports 185 changed-path tests across 11 files, and a rendered contrast audit covering 15,292 visible text runs across 16 theme scopes and 14 screen states with no text below the configured WCAG floor. It also records UI smoke coverage at 1440, 390, and 320 pixel widths in both light and dark modes. The current task check will revalidate the branch after the report repair.

## Approaches tried

The UI changes stay local to the controls that lacked names. The close button uses the dialog primitive's supported `aria-label`; the skills button keeps its visible icon and adds a dynamic label based on the agent role. This preserves the compact visual treatment while giving assistive technology useful action names. The tests focus on those exposed names, keeping the regression assertion close to the defect.

For QA evidence, the branch contains both the written keyboard observations and the test/audit results. The task's declared screenshot set is also present in its task metadata. A previous handoff attempt found that the Agents shot's unscoped `.agent-skills-add` selector matched multiple cards and therefore could not identify the engineer button. That selector was narrowed to the engineer's accessible name, and the activity log subsequently records that all four declared shots were captured with a clean console. This addresses the shot-capture ambiguity without weakening the selector.

## Challenges and blockers

The immediate blocker on this resumed turn was the report schema: the prior draft only described a close-out repair and omitted all five required headings. The report has now been rewritten to include each section and explain the underlying implementation and recorded QA evidence.

This turn did not repeat the interactive keyboard session. The QA note and task activity are the source for the prior route walkthrough; this report distinguishes those earlier results from current-session observations. The branch had already been through multiple checks and review cycles. A close-out repair merged main and resolved a duplicate property in `servers-command.test.ts`; the task history records a successful full check after that repair. The requested scoped check remains the required final gate for this handoff attempt.

## Key learnings

Icon-only controls need explicit accessible names even when they have a visible glyph or a `title`. Role-specific names also matter when the same control appears repeatedly in a list: “Add skills to engineer” is more actionable than a generic “Add skills.”

Keyboard behavior should be recorded as observable behavior by route and control. A focus trap, Escape dismissal, and focus restoration are separate outcomes; inline disclosures should not be treated as dialogs just because they reveal content. Finally, screenshot steps must target a unique element. In this task, the accessible-name selector both disambiguates the intended card and states what action the button performs.

The current turn repairs the report-only handoff issue; it makes no additional product changes. RepoOS can bind this report to the checked tree once the scoped check passes.
